items.stem: A company moved a monolithic application into containers that run as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate. The task definition names a task role and a task execution role. Neither role has any permissions yet. Company policy says that every component must follow the principle of least privilege. The application code in the container must read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket. Which change will allow this in the MOST secure way?
keywords: The application code in the container must read objects

options.text: Add the needed permissions to the task role that the task definition names, and keep the task execution role unchanged.
options.why: The task role [allows your application code (running in the container)](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-gives-app-code-aws-permissions) to call other AWS services such as Amazon S3.

options.text: Add the needed permissions to the task execution role that the task definition names, and keep the task role unchanged.
options.why: The task execution role serves the agents, and its permissions [aren't directly accessible by the containers](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-execution-role-for-agents), so the application code cannot use them.

options.text: Create an EC2 instance profile with the needed permissions, and attach the instance profile to the Fargate tasks of the service.
options.why: On Fargate, [EC2 instance profiles are not available](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-fargate-no-instance-profile) for the containers of a task, so there is nothing to attach.
options.misconception: gives containers on Fargate their credentials through an EC2 instance profile

options.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to both the task role and the task execution role that the task definition names.
options.why: It works, but it gives every component full access, and AWS advises the [minimum required permissions for the tasks to operate](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-least-privilege-per-task-definition).

items.explanation: The application code needs AWS permissions, so the permissions go to the task role. The task role [allows your application code (running in the container)](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-gives-app-code-aws-permissions) to use AWS services. The task execution role [grants the Amazon ECS container and Fargate agents](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-execution-role-for-agents) their permissions instead. The change adds the S3 read and nothing else, which keeps least privilege.
items.takeaway: Application code calls AWS with the task role; the agents pull images and send logs with the task execution role.
items.twin: If the stem said "The tasks must pull the container image from a private Amazon ECR repository" instead: the task execution role, because the [container agent must have permissions](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-ecs-agent-pull-permissions) for the pull.
items.say: The code in the container needs S3, so the permission goes on the task role, not the execution role.

solvers.stem_only: The application code uses the task role (task IAM role) for its AWS API calls. Grant only s3:GetObject (and ListBucket if needed) on that bucket to the task role; the task execution role is for the ECS agent (image pull, logs, secrets) and stays empty.

items.stem: A company runs all its Kubernetes pods on Amazon EKS with AWS Fargate. The cluster is serverless today, and the teams deploy with Kubernetes manifests. A new compliance rule requires a log agent next to every application container. The company wants to keep all pods on Fargate and does not want to manage nodes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: a log agent next to every application container

options.text: Deploy the log agent as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, so that one agent pod runs next to the application pods on every Fargate node.
options.why: [Daemonsets aren’t supported on Fargate](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-no-daemonsets) in Amazon EKS, so the agent pods never run next to the application pods.

options.text: Build the log agent into the image of each application container, so that one container runs both the application and the agent.
options.why: It works, but each agent update then means a rebuild and a new test of every application image by every team.
options.misconception: bundling the agent into each application image is the simplest way

options.text: Add the log agent as a sidecar container to the pod specification of each application, so that every pod runs its own agent.
options.why: For a daemon on Fargate, AWS says to reconfigure it to [run as a sidecar container](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-no-daemonsets) in the pods, and the agent image stays separate.

options.text: Add the log agent to the Fargate profile, so that Fargate starts the agent in every pod that the profile selects.
options.why: A Fargate profile only selects pods: they are [matched using a namespace and the labels](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-profile-selects-pods), and the profile adds no containers.
options.misconception: a Fargate profile can add containers to the pods it selects

items.explanation: Fargate [runs only one Pod per node](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-pod-own-compute-boundary), and [Daemonsets aren’t supported on Fargate](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-no-daemonsets). The documented fix is to [run as a sidecar container](../facts/eks.md#eks-fargate-no-daemonsets) in each pod. The sidecar is a second container in the same pod, so the application images stay unchanged and every pod gets its agent.
items.takeaway: EKS on Fargate runs no DaemonSets: run a per-pod agent as a sidecar container.
items.twin: If the stem said "the pods run on a managed node group" instead: a DaemonSet, because it makes sure that the agent [runs on every node in your cluster](../facts/eks.md#eks-daemonset-runs-on-every-node).
items.say: On Fargate there are no DaemonSets, so the log agent runs as a sidecar in each pod.

solvers.stem_only: DaemonSets do not run on EKS Fargate because there are no nodes to manage. Run the log agent as a sidecar container in each pod spec (keep application and agent as separate containers).

items.stem: A company runs an uploaded document processing service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. The tasks run across multiple Availability Zones. Each task writes working files that other tasks pick up later. All tasks must read and write the same set of files, and the files must be durable when Amazon ECS replaces a task. Which storage solution will meet these requirements?
keywords: All tasks must read and write the same set of files
durable when Amazon ECS replaces a task

options.text: Increase the ephemeral storage of each task to the largest size that Fargate allows, and write the files to that storage.
options.why: Ephemeral storage starts at [20 GiB](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-faq-ephemeral-storage-20-gib-erased) per task, and its data is erased when the task stops, at any size.

options.text: Attach an Amazon EBS volume to each task of the service, and write the files to the volume of that task.
options.why: EBS volumes of service tasks are [always deleted upon task termination](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-ebs-volume-service-task-deleted-on-termination), and each task gets a volume of its own.

options.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system, and mount the file system as a volume in the task definition of the service.
options.why: EFS gives tasks [access to the same persistent storage](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-efs-volumes-shared-persistent-across-instances) wherever they run, so all tasks share the files and the files outlive any task.

options.text: Define a bind mount that the containers of each task share, and write the files to that bind mount.
options.why: Fargate supports [bind mounts for ephemeral storage](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-storage-types-ebs-efs-bind): the containers of one task share them, but other tasks do not see them.
options.misconception: a bind mount is shared between tasks and survives the task

items.explanation: The files need two things: sharing between tasks and durability after a task ends. On Fargate, [Amazon Elastic File System (EFS)](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-faq-efs-for-persistent-storage) provides persistent storage. Every task that mounts the file system gets [access to the same persistent storage](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-efs-volumes-shared-persistent-across-instances), in any Availability Zone.
items.takeaway: Files that many tasks share and that outlive each task: Amazon EFS, not task storage.
items.twin: If the stem said "each task needs scratch space for its own temporary files" instead: ephemeral storage, because Fargate gives each workload [20 GiB](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-faq-ephemeral-storage-20-gib-erased) of temporary storage.
items.say: Shared files that must survive task replacement go on EFS, mounted by every task.

solvers.stem_only: Use Amazon EFS as a shared, multi-AZ, durable file system mounted as a volume in the Fargate task definition; ephemeral storage, bind mounts and per-task EBS volumes are not shared and do not survive task replacement.

items.stem: A company stores a containerized job in Amazon ECR. The job processes recorded calls. The job starts at sporadic times, when a customer asks for a bulk export. Each run is long-running and takes 2 to 3 hours. An application already starts each run through an API call. The company does not want to manage servers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: does not want to manage servers

options.text: Package the job as a container image for an AWS Lambda function, and raise the function timeout through a Service Quotas request.
options.why: Lambda allows [15 minutes per invocation](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit) at most, and the timeout is a configuration quota: [except as noted, they can't be changed](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-config-quotas-not-changeable).

options.text: Launch an Amazon EC2 instance that runs all day, and start each export run on the instance with a script that the application calls.
options.why: It works, but the company then manages, patches and pays for an instance that waits idle between the sporadic runs.

options.text: Run the job as an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate, and have the application start one task for each export request.
options.why: With Fargate you [run containers without having to manage servers](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-fargate-no-servers-for-containers), and Fargate has [no hard limit on execution time](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit) for a long run.

options.text: Create an Amazon EKS cluster with a managed node group, and run each export as a Kubernetes job in a pod on the nodes.
options.why: It works, but with managed node groups you [must deploy and manage Amazon EC2 instances](../facts/eks.md#eks-compute-compare-who-manages-ec2-instances), and the nodes wait between the sporadic runs.
options.misconception: a managed node group removes all server management

items.explanation: Each run takes hours, more than the [15 minutes per invocation](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit) of Lambda, and the company wants no servers. A Fargate task fits, because Fargate suits [long-running applications, microservices, or batch processing](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-long-running-lambda-short). The task ends when the run ends, so nothing waits between sporadic runs.
items.takeaway: A container job of hours with no servers to manage: an ECS task on Fargate, not Lambda.
items.twin: If the stem said "each run takes 2 to 3 minutes" instead: a Lambda function from the container image, because Lambda functions suit [short-lived, event-driven tasks](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-long-running-lambda-short).
items.say: A job of hours with no servers: run it as an ECS task on Fargate, because Lambda stops at fifteen minutes.

solvers.stem_only: Lambda tops out at 15 minutes and cannot be raised, so a 2-3 hour job needs containers. Run it as a standalone ECS task on Fargate started by the application with RunTask for each request; no servers, no idle cost.

items.stem: A company runs a web application as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate. The company does not want to manage instances. At a minimum, two tasks must run at all times. During the day, service auto scaling adds more tasks, and the number of extra tasks changes from hour to hour. The extra tasks can tolerate interruption. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: two tasks must run at all times
The extra tasks can tolerate interruption

options.text: Use a capacity provider strategy with FARGATE_SPOT only, and set the minimum task count of service auto scaling to 2.
options.why: The minimum count does not choose the capacity, and [Fargate doesn't replace Spot capacity with on-demand capacity](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-no-on-demand-replacement), so the two tasks can stop together.

options.text: Use a capacity provider strategy with a base of 2 tasks on FARGATE and the larger weight on FARGATE_SPOT.
options.why: The base keeps the first two tasks on FARGATE, and the weight sends most extra tasks to FARGATE_SPOT, at [up to a 70 percent discount](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-faq-spot-up-to-70-percent-discount).

options.text: Use a capacity provider strategy with FARGATE only, and buy a Compute Savings Plan that covers the Fargate usage of the service.
options.why: It works, but Savings Plans are [a better fit for steady-state workloads](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline), and the extra tasks vary from hour to hour and can stop.

options.text: Move the service to an Auto Scaling group capacity provider of EC2 Spot Instances, and give that capacity provider a base of 2 tasks.
options.why: Spot Instances do not protect the base: [Amazon EC2 can interrupt your Spot Instance when it needs it back](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-interruption-reasons), and the company would manage instances.

items.explanation: Split the service by need. The stem needs two steady tasks, so the base keeps them on FARGATE. The extra tasks can stop, so the weight sends most of them to FARGATE_SPOT, which can [run interruption tolerant Amazon ECS tasks](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-interruption-tolerant-discount) at a discount. Fargate Spot alone is risky, because [Fargate doesn't replace Spot capacity with on-demand capacity](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-no-on-demand-replacement).
items.takeaway: A steady minimum goes in the base on FARGATE; the interruptible extra tasks go to FARGATE_SPOT.
items.twin: If the stem said "all tasks can tolerate interruption" instead: FARGATE_SPOT for all tasks, because it runs tasks at a rate [discounted compared to the Fargate price](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-interruption-tolerant-discount).
items.say: Put the minimum in the base on regular Fargate and send the rest to Fargate Spot.

solvers.stem_only: Capacity provider strategy with FARGATE base 2 (the always-on minimum, not interruptible) and FARGATE_SPOT carrying the higher weight for the variable, interruption-tolerant extra tasks.

items.stem: A company runs 20 tasks of a data processing service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. The service reads jobs from a queue and writes the results to Amazon S3. The company does not want to manage instances. The tasks process intermittent batch work and can be stopped and restarted at any time without harm. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: can be stopped and restarted at any time without harm

options.text: Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider at the standard Fargate price, with no commitment and no other change.
options.why: The standard price works, but it pays the full Fargate price for work that [can tolerate interruptions](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline) and could run at the Spot rate.

options.text: Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider, and buy a Compute Savings Plan that covers the Fargate usage of the tasks.
options.why: A Compute Savings Plan works, but Savings Plans are [a better fit for steady-state workloads](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline), and intermittent work leaves the committed spend unused in idle hours.
options.misconception: a commitment saves money on any load, also an intermittent one

options.text: Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider, and buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the instance family that Fargate uses.
options.why: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan does not fit: these plans cover [a specific instance family within a Region](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility); it is Compute Savings Plans that [also cover Fargate and Lambda usage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility).
options.misconception: an EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers Fargate usage

options.text: Move the tasks to the FARGATE_SPOT capacity provider at the Fargate Spot price, with no commitment and no other change.
options.why: Fargate Spot is for tasks that tolerate interruption, and it runs them at a rate [discounted compared to the Fargate price](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-interruption-tolerant-discount).

items.explanation: The tasks can stop and restart without harm, and the work is intermittent. Fargate Spot can [run interruption tolerant Amazon ECS tasks](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-interruption-tolerant-discount) at [up to a 70 percent discount](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-faq-spot-up-to-70-percent-discount) off the Fargate price, with no commitment. When AWS needs the capacity back, a task gets a [two-minute warning](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-two-minute-interruption-warning) and restarts later.
items.takeaway: Interruptible, intermittent Fargate work: FARGATE_SPOT. Steady, uninterrupted Fargate work: a Compute Savings Plan.
items.twin: If the stem said "The tasks serve a steady-state load all day, every day, and must not be interrupted" instead: the Compute Savings Plan, because Savings Plans are [a better fit for steady-state workloads](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline).
items.say: Work that can stop and restart, with gaps: Fargate Spot, no commitment.

solvers.stem_only: Interruption-tolerant, intermittent batch work on Fargate: run on Fargate Spot (FARGATE_SPOT capacity provider); no commitment because usage is not steady.

items.stem: A company plans to migrate its containerized applications to Amazon ECS. The applications use public base images from Docker Hub. Security rules require that the tasks pull every image from Amazon ECR. A one-time copy of the images is not enough, because the images in ECR must stay current when new versions appear in Docker Hub. Which solution will meet these requirements?
keywords: pull every image from Amazon ECR
must stay current when new versions appear in Docker Hub

options.text: Pull each image from Docker Hub one time, push the image to a private ECR repository, and point the task definitions at the copies.
options.why: After [a one-time copy of container images](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-migrate-one-time-copy-no-auto-update), newer versions in Docker Hub [are not pulled automatically](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-migrate-one-time-copy-no-auto-update).
options.misconception: a one-time copy into ECR picks up new upstream versions

options.text: Create an ECR replication rule that uses Docker Hub as the source registry and the private ECR registry as the destination.
options.why: Replication copies images between ECR registries: [Amazon ECR supports both cross-Region and cross-account replication](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-replication-cross-region-cross-account) of a private registry, not copies from Docker Hub.
options.misconception: ECR replication can copy images from an outside registry

options.text: Keep the images in Docker Hub, and give the tasks a route through a NAT gateway so that each task pulls the latest image.
options.why: It keeps the images current, but the tasks then pull from Docker Hub, not from Amazon ECR, which breaks the security rule.
options.misconception: pulling the source images directly meets a rule that names ECR

options.text: Create an ECR pull through cache rule for Docker Hub, store the Docker Hub credentials in a Secrets Manager secret, and use the cached images.
options.why: The rule lets ECR [cache repositories in an upstream registry](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-pull-through-cache-keeps-cache-current) such as Docker Hub, and the tasks pull the cached images from ECR.

items.explanation: A pull through cache rule lets ECR [cache repositories in an upstream registry](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-pull-through-cache-keeps-cache-current) in the private registry. ECR will [periodically reach out to the upstream registry](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-pull-through-cache-keeps-cache-current) so that the cached image stays up to date. The Secrets Manager secret holds the Docker Hub credentials that the rule signs in with. The tasks pull from ECR, and new Docker Hub versions arrive without a manual copy.
items.takeaway: ECR images that follow an outside registry: a pull through cache rule. A one-time copy does not update.
items.twin: If the stem said "the images already sit in an ECR private registry in another Region" instead: ECR replication, because [Amazon ECR supports both cross-Region and cross-account replication](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-replication-cross-region-cross-account).
items.say: To keep Docker Hub images current inside ECR, I'd create a pull through cache rule.

solvers.stem_only: ECR pull through cache rule with Docker Hub as upstream; Docker Hub needs credentials stored in a Secrets Manager secret. Tasks pull through the ECR cache URI and ECR keeps the cached images in sync with the upstream.

items.stem: A company moved a monolithic application into containers that run as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate. The task definition names a task role and a task execution role. Neither role has any permissions yet. Company policy says that every component must follow the principle of least privilege. The tasks must pull the container image from a private Amazon ECR repository. Which change will allow this in the MOST secure way?
keywords: must pull the container image from a private Amazon ECR repository

options.text: Add the needed permissions to the task role that the task definition names, and keep the task execution role unchanged.
options.why: Task role permissions [aren't accessed by the Amazon ECS container](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-gives-app-code-aws-permissions) agent, and the agent is what pulls the image.
options.misconception: the task role gives the agent its image pull permissions

options.text: Add the needed permissions to the task execution role that the task definition names, and keep the task role unchanged.
options.why: The [container agent must have permissions](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-ecs-agent-pull-permissions) to pull from ECR, and the task execution role [grants the Amazon ECS container and Fargate agents](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-execution-role-for-agents) their permissions.

options.text: Create an EC2 instance profile with the needed permissions, and attach the instance profile to the Fargate tasks of the service.
options.why: On Fargate, [EC2 instance profiles are not available](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-fargate-no-instance-profile) for the containers of a task, so there is nothing to attach.
options.misconception: gives tasks on Fargate their pull permissions through an EC2 instance profile

options.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to both the task role and the task execution role that the task definition names.
options.why: It works, but it gives every component full access, and AWS advises the [minimum required permissions for the tasks to operate](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-least-privilege-per-task-definition).

items.explanation: The image pull happens before the container starts, so the application code is not involved. A task on Fargate that pulls a container image from [an Amazon ECR private repository](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-execution-role-use-cases) needs the task execution role. The change adds the ECR pull permissions to that role and nothing else, which keeps least privilege.
items.takeaway: The image pull belongs to the agent, so its permissions go on the task execution role, not the task role.
items.twin: If the stem said "The application code in the container must read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket" instead: the task role, because it [allows your application code (running in the container)](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-task-role-gives-app-code-aws-permissions) to use AWS services.
items.say: The agent pulls the image, so the ECR permissions go on the task execution role.

solvers.stem_only: Image pulls from private ECR are made by the ECS agent / Fargate on behalf of the task using the task execution role. Grant the ECR pull permissions (GetAuthorizationToken, BatchGetImage, GetDownloadUrlForLayer, BatchCheckLayerAvailability) to the task execution role only.

items.stem: A company runs an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate in private subnets. Stringent security rules forbid any route from these subnets to the internet, and the security team reviews every resource that the company adds to the VPC. An internal Application Load Balancer must send requests to the tasks, and the tasks must pull their container image privately from Amazon ECR. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: forbid any route from these subnets to the internet
pull their container image privately from Amazon ECR
reviews every resource that the company adds to the VPC

options.text: Create interface VPC endpoints for the Amazon ECR API and the Docker registry, and create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3.
options.why: Fargate tasks [require both Amazon ECR VPC endpoints](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3) and [the Amazon S3 gateway endpoint](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3) to pull privately.

options.text: Create the target group of the load balancer with the instance target type, and attach the target group to the ECS service.
options.why: Fargate tasks are [associated with an elastic network interface](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-target-group-ip-target-type), not with an EC2 instance, so the instance target type does not fit them.

options.text: Turn on public IP address assignment for the tasks, so that the tasks reach Amazon ECR without a route to an internet gateway.
options.why: A task with a public IP address still needs a [route to the internet or a NAT gateway](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-public-subnet-image-pull-needs-public-ip) to pull, and the rules forbid that route.

options.text: Create the target group of the load balancer with the ip target type, and attach the target group to the ECS service.
options.why: Fargate tasks are [associated with an elastic network interface](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-target-group-ip-target-type), so the target group registers the IP address of each task.

options.text: Create interface VPC endpoints for every AWS service that offers them in the Region, and create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3.
options.why: It works, because the set includes the ECR and S3 endpoints, but every extra endpoint is one more resource for the security team to review and manage.

items.explanation: For the image, Fargate tasks [require both Amazon ECR VPC endpoints](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3) and [the Amazon S3 gateway endpoint](../facts/ecr.md#ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3), and the pull then runs [over the task's private IPv4 address](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-ecr-endpoint-uses-private-ip). For the load balancer, each task has its own network interface, so the target group uses ip targets.
items.takeaway: Private Fargate tasks behind a load balancer: ECR and S3 endpoints for the pull, ip targets for the traffic.
items.twin: If the stem said "the tasks run in public subnets that route to an internet gateway" instead: public IP addresses on the tasks work for the pull, because in a public subnet [a public IP address needs to be assigned](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-public-subnet-image-pull-needs-public-ip).
items.say: No internet route: ECR endpoints plus the S3 gateway endpoint for the pull, and ip targets for the load balancer.

solvers.stem_only: Fargate tasks use awsvpc networking, so the ALB target group must use the ip target type. For a private image pull with no internet route, create interface VPC endpoints for com.amazonaws.region.ecr.api and ecr.dkr, plus an S3 gateway endpoint (image layers are stored in S3); only the endpoints needed, to keep the security review small. No public IPs, no NAT.

items.stem: A company runs its applications on a self-managed Kubernetes cluster in its data center. The cluster runs on servers that are near the end of their life. The teams want to keep deploying with their Kubernetes manifests and kubectl. The company plans to migrate the applications to AWS with minimal code changes, and it does not want to refactor them. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: keep deploying with their Kubernetes manifests and kubectl

options.text: Create an Amazon EKS cluster with managed node groups, and deploy the existing Kubernetes manifests to the cluster with kubectl.
options.why: Amazon EKS is a [natural migration path if you use Kubernetes already](../facts/eks.md#eks-whitepaper-natural-migration-path-for-kubernetes), and [it manages the control plane for you](../facts/eks.md#eks-managed-control-plane-across-azs).

options.text: Rewrite the Kubernetes manifests as Amazon ECS task definitions, and run the applications as ECS services on AWS Fargate.
options.why: Fargate removes the nodes, but the teams lose their manifests and kubectl, and every deployment needs a rewrite for Amazon ECS.
options.misconception: a serverless rewrite always has less overhead than a move to managed Kubernetes

options.text: Install Kubernetes on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group, and deploy the existing Kubernetes manifests to that cluster.
options.why: It works, but the company then runs the control plane itself, and Amazon EKS [automatically detects and replaces unhealthy control plane nodes](../facts/eks.md#eks-faq-control-plane-multi-az-and-self-healing).

options.text: Install Amazon EKS Anywhere on Amazon EC2 instances in a VPC, and deploy the existing Kubernetes manifests to that cluster.
options.why: Amazon EKS Anywhere is [not supported on AWS Cloud](../facts/eks-anywhere.md#eks-anywhere-faq-not-supported-on-aws-cloud), so it does not run on EC2 instances in a VPC.
options.misconception: EKS Anywhere can run on EC2 instances in the AWS Cloud

items.explanation: The applications already run on standard Kubernetes, and the teams keep their manifests. Standard Kubernetes applications move to Amazon EKS [without any code modifications](../facts/eks.md#eks-faq-migrate-standard-kubernetes-without-code-changes). Amazon EKS is a [managed service](../facts/eks.md#eks-faq-managed-kubernetes-no-control-plane-to-run) that runs the control plane, so the company operates only the node groups.
items.takeaway: Existing Kubernetes, no refactor, no control plane to run: Amazon EKS.
items.twin: If the stem said "the clusters must stay in the company's own data center" instead: Amazon EKS Anywhere, because its clusters [run entirely on your infrastructure](../facts/eks.md#eks-faq-anywhere-clusters-run-entirely-on-your-infrastructure).
items.say: They already use Kubernetes, so EKS keeps their manifests and takes the control plane off their hands.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: the applications already run on Kubernetes, the teams keep their manifests and kubectl, the move needs minimal code changes, and the company does not want to refactor.
Before I look at the options, I predict Amazon EKS, because it runs standard Kubernetes applications without code changes and AWS manages the control plane.
I remove the rewrite to ECS task definitions, because the teams would lose their manifests and kubectl. I remove EKS Anywhere on EC2 instances, because EKS Anywhere is not supported on the AWS Cloud.

Between Amazon EKS and Kubernetes installed on EC2 instances the difference is who runs the control plane; the stem asks for the LEAST operational overhead, so the managed control plane of EKS decides it.
Check: an EKS cluster with managed node groups keeps the manifests and kubectl, needs no code changes, and removes the control plane work from the company. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Move to Amazon EKS (managed control plane) with managed node groups (or Fargate) and keep using the existing manifests and kubectl; EKS Anywhere is for on-premises, self-managed Kubernetes on EC2 adds overhead, ECS needs a rewrite.

items.stem: A company runs 20 tasks of a data processing service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. The service reads jobs from a queue and writes the results to Amazon S3. The company does not want to manage instances. The tasks serve a steady-state load all day, every day, and must not be interrupted. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: steady-state load all day, every day

options.text: Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider at the standard Fargate price, with no commitment and no other change.
options.why: It works, but a steady load at the standard price costs more than the same load under a Compute Savings Plan, which can [apply to your Fargate and Lambda usage](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-compute-savings-plans-cover-fargate-lambda).

options.text: Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider, and buy a Compute Savings Plan that covers the Fargate usage of the tasks.
options.why: Compute Savings Plans [apply to your Fargate and Lambda usage](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-compute-savings-plans-cover-fargate-lambda), and Savings Plans are [a better fit for steady-state workloads](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline) that run all day.

options.text: Keep the tasks on the FARGATE capacity provider, and buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the instance family that Fargate uses.
options.why: EC2 Instance Savings Plans cover [a specific instance family within a Region](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility); it is Compute Savings Plans that [also cover Fargate and Lambda usage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility).
options.misconception: an EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers Fargate usage

options.text: Move the tasks to the FARGATE_SPOT capacity provider at the Fargate Spot price, with no commitment and no other change.
options.why: Fargate Spot tasks get a [two-minute warning](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-two-minute-interruption-warning) and stop when AWS needs the capacity back, which breaks the no-interruption requirement.

items.explanation: The load is steady and the stem rules out interruptions, so Spot is out. Fargate supports [Spot and Compute Savings Plan pricing options](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-faq-spot-and-compute-savings-plan-pricing). A Compute Savings Plan lowers the price of steady Fargate usage in exchange for a commitment, and Savings Plans are [a better fit for steady-state workloads](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline).
items.takeaway: Steady Fargate load that has to run without interruption: a Compute Savings Plan, not FARGATE_SPOT.
items.twin: If the stem said "The tasks process intermittent batch work and can be stopped and restarted at any time without harm" instead: FARGATE_SPOT, because it runs tasks at a rate [discounted compared to the Fargate price](../facts/fargate.md#fargate-spot-interruption-tolerant-discount).
items.say: Steady load all day that must not stop: a Compute Savings Plan on Fargate, not Spot.

solvers.stem_only: Steady, uninterruptible Fargate usage: keep on-demand FARGATE and buy a Compute Savings Plan, which applies to Fargate (EC2 Instance Savings Plans do not; Spot can be interrupted).

items.stem: A company runs an Amazon ECS service on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The group has sufficient instances for the day peak. At night, service auto scaling lowers the task count, but the number of instances stays the same, and most instances run few tasks. The company wants to stop paying for idle instances at night. Which combination of steps is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
keywords: the number of instances stays the same

options.text: Lower the minimum task count of the service auto scaling policy, so that service auto scaling also removes the idle instances.
options.why: Service auto scaling can [increase or decrease the desired number](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-service-auto-scaling-application-auto-scaling) of tasks, not of instances, and the task count already drops at night.

options.text: Change the task placement strategy of the service to binpack on memory, so that the tasks fill as few instances as possible.
options.why: Binpack leaves [the least amount of unused CPU or memory](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-placement-binpack-least-unused-cpu-memory) on each instance, so the tasks fill fewer instances and free the rest for removal.

options.text: Change the task placement strategy of the service to spread on instance ID, so that each instance runs a share of the tasks.
options.why: Spread [spreads placement across available candidates evenly](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-placement-strategy-types-binpack-random-spread), so tasks stay on every instance and no instance becomes free to remove.
options.misconception: spreading the tasks thin lets the cluster remove instances

options.text: Add an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling to the capacity provider strategy of the service, with a target capacity of 50 percent to keep spare instances.
options.why: It scales in, but a target below full use keeps [the amount of free capacity](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-target-capacity-below-100-keeps-spare-instances) as idle instances, which costs more at night.

options.text: Add an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling to the capacity provider strategy of the service, with a target capacity of 100 percent.
options.why: Managed scaling lets Amazon ECS [manage the scaling of Amazon EC2 instances](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-managed-scaling-asg-capacity-provider), so the group can [terminate EC2 container instances, and then deregister them](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-reservation-above-or-below-target).

items.explanation: Two gaps exist. The instances do not follow the task count, so cluster auto scaling is missing: managed scaling lets Amazon ECS [manage the scaling of Amazon EC2 instances](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-managed-scaling-asg-capacity-provider). The tasks are spread thin, so no instance is empty: binpack [minimizes the number of container instances in use](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-placement-binpack-least-unused-cpu-memory).
items.takeaway: Tasks drop but instances stay: add cluster auto scaling through managed scaling, and binpack the tasks.
items.twin: If the stem said "the service runs on AWS Fargate" instead: no instance step is needed, because for Fargate [AWS manages and automatically scales the underlying capacity](../facts/ecs.md#ecs-predictive-scaling-service-level-not-compute).
items.say: Service auto scaling moves tasks, not instances: turn on managed scaling and binpack the tasks.

solvers.stem_only: Use an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling (target capacity 100 percent, so no spare instances are kept) in the service's capacity provider strategy, so ECS scales the group in when instances are idle; and use a binpack placement strategy (on memory or CPU) so tasks fill as few instances as possible and the rest become empty and can be removed.
